title: Batangas City holds 'bokashi ball' throwing for river restoration
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - The Batangas City government led a "bokashi ball" throwing event at Calumpang Bridge as part of its efforts to rehabilitate the river and improve its water quality.

Held as part of the city's 57th Foundation Day celebration, hurling "bokashi balls" aims to restore river quality, strengthen environmental protection measures, and encourage greater community participation in keeping local waterways clean, the City Public Information Office (PIO) said in a report on Tuesday.

"Bokashi balls", also known as mud balls, originated in Japan, where they are widely used to revive polluted waterways.

READ: Bayanihan and corporate social impact

They contain beneficial microorganisms that help break down organic waste, reduce foul odors, and decompose sludge accumulated in contaminated bodies of water, the PIO said, citing City Environment Officer Oliver Gonzales. Bokashi balls can also help improve soil quality.

According to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), a single bokashi ball can help treat approximately one cubic meter of sludge-laden water. This form of biotechnology has been used across the country, such as in the Manila Bay watershed.

"Through programs such as this, the Batangas City government continues to promote a clean, safe, and greener environment for the benefit of both present and future generations," the PIO said.

The Calumpang River has a catchment area of about 472 square kilometers. It forms the southeastern boundary of Batangas City's urban center before emptying into Batangas Bay.

Local authorities said the river has faced increasing environmental pressure from rapid urbanization and agricultural runoff over the years, prompting the implementation of watershed protection measures and river cleanup initiatives./coa

title: Helping communities grow together
content_lead:
FIFTY-NINE residents of Barangay Sorosoro Ibaba in Batangas pooled together P11,800 in 1969 to put up a small community store. Today, that organization has grown into the Sorosoro Ibaba Development Cooperative (SIDC), one of the country's largest agri-based cooperatives with more than 81,000 members, operations spanning agriculture, financial services, retail and wholesale, and assets of about P7.7 billion.

SIDC is not an isolated success story. The Ayala Coop which traces its roots to 1995, when 21 employees of the Ayala Group organized the cooperative with an initial capital of P10,500. Since then, it has expanded into one of the country's largest employee-owned cooperatives, with nearly 40,000 members nationwide, capitalization exceeding P5 billion and total assets of more than P6 billion.

For the past 36 years, the CDA has been the government's lead agency for the cooperative sector. Created through Republic Act 6939 in 1990, it was tasked with promoting the growth of cooperatives while ensuring they remain faithful to the principles on which they were founded. While registration and regulation remain at the heart of its mandate, the agency also provides technical assistance, promotes good governance and works with local governments and national agencies to help cooperatives expand.

Since assuming the chairmanship in 2025, Undersecretary Alexander B. Raquepo has placed much of the agency's attention on expanding support for micro and small cooperatives, improving coordination with local governments and national agencies, and carrying out the Philippine Cooperative Development Plan 2025-2028. Those priorities have shaped many of the programs introduced this year.

Working alongside the CDA Board, Administrator Emmanuel Santiaguel oversees the day-to-day implementation of the agency's programs, from cooperative registration and regulation to education, technical assistance and field operations carried out through its regional offices.

title: Giant clams survive, thrive in Batangas marine sanctuaries
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- Giant clams (Tridacna gigas) seeded in the municipal waters off Lian and Nasugbu in Batangas province more than a decade ago continue to survive and thrive in protected marine areas.

In a report on Friday, Aug. 7, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR)-Calabarzon said giant clams planted in 2015 and 2016 in locally managed marine sanctuaries and protected areas in the two municipalities remain healthy.

The giant clams were seeded through the efforts of the DENR's Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) in Calaca in partnership with local communities and other stakeholders.

READ: Cadiz City goes after giant clams' killers

"Based on the latest monitoring, the giant clams have reached an average length of 2.25 feet," the DENR said.

The agency said the giant clams remain safe within the marine sanctuaries through the continuing protection and monitoring efforts of CENRO-Calaca and its local partners.

Locally known as "taklobo," the giant clam is the world's largest bivalve mollusk. It is classified as critically endangered on the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

Giant clams are also protected under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), an international agreement among governments designed to ensure that trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival.

The harvesting, selling, purchasing, and transporting of giant clams is prohibited under Republic Act No. 10654, or the Philippine Fisheries Code.

Beyond their value as food, giant clams are also targeted for their massive shells, which have been used as materials for jewelry, chandeliers, religious icons and other products.

Their valuable shells have made the endangered species a target of illegal trade, with some smugglers reportedly turning to giant clams as substitutes for ivory.

title: Coming Full Circle: From 4Ps Beneficiary To CPA, Public Servant | Journal Online

Aina Lou Atienza is a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) and Municipal Accountant in her hometown of San Nicolas, Batangas.

Instead, Aina sees the faces of her own family reflected in the records of the indigent citizens they aim to uplift.

Long before Aina became a department head who helped steer the town's social programs, she was at the receiving end of the programs.

Past forged by struggles

Aina's journey into public service was forged in the quiet struggles of a farming family.

"Yung tanim ng father ko ay kamote. So, 9 months to 1 year bago po mag harvest. So, talagang merong times na 'yung tindahan lang 'yung source of income ng buong pamilya," Aina recalled.

title: Bacoor City suspends classes as monsoon rains persist
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - The local government of Bacoor City in Cavite suspended classes at all levels in public and private schools on Tuesday (August 11), due to the continuing inclement weather.

The city government urged residents to prioritize their safety, stay indoors as much as possible, and to continue monitoring official weather and government advisories.

READ: Walang pasok: Class, work suspensions on Aug. 11

The suspension is consistent with the provisions of Department of Education (DepEd) Order No. 37, series of 2022, which provides for the automatic suspension of classes at all levels, whether face-to-face or online, when the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) issues a tropical cyclone wind signal, an orange or red rainfall warning, or a flood warning.

Classes are likewise suspended when any of these warnings or signals are issued while classes are already ongoing.

Local chief executives may also suspend classes in their respective jurisdictions whenever weather conditions pose a risk to students and school personnel, even in the absence of an automatic suspension.

Pagasa forecast that heavy rains associated with the enhanced southwest monsoon, or "habagat", would continue until Wednesday (August 12) although rainfall is expected to gradually weaken beginning Tuesday.

The weather bureau urged the public, particularly residents in affected areas, to remain vigilant and rely on official advisories issued by government agencies.

Meanwhile, another weather disturbance, Tropical Storm Peilou, was being monitored outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility. /jpv

Cavite has seen rapid expansion of commercial establishments, infrastructure, expressways and road networks in recent years, improving connectivity and generating economic activity.

Despite the development, flooding remains a recurring problem in several communities, leaving some residents to improvise their own defenses whenever rivers and waterways overflow.

title: 4 tons of mishandled meat seized in Cavite
content_lead:
Authorities seized 4 tons of mishandled meat at a wet market in Dasmariñas, Cavite early Wednesday.

In a "24 Oras" report from James Augustin, several boxes from a parked refrigerated van were inspected by the joint forces of the National Meat Inspection Service (NMIS) and the Philippine National Police Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (PNP CIDG).

Authorities found that the van's freezer was not working, and the meat they were transporting had gone soft. They were also able to find frozen meat that had become rotten.

"'Yung box po kasi talaga 'yung karton madali lang talaga masira. Pero tingnan n'yo 'yung ano namin, matitigas po 'yan kahit hawakan n'yo po 'yang pige na 'yan," said one of the vendors of the frozen meat.

(The cardboard box itself is really fragile and easily damaged. But look at it -- it's very firm, just try to press on it.)

The vendor admitted that the refrigerator of the van is working, but that it was turned off.

NMIS Region 4A Director Eduardo Oblena said the mishandled meat could also be considered "hot meat".

"The standard maintaining temperature of our frozen meat is minus 18 degrees centigrade," Oblena said.

Authorities also seized frozen meat that was on display and not stored in a freezer or chiller. They ended up confiscating 4 tons of hot meat. Those caught selling the mishandled meat were issued a confiscation report.

The confiscated meat was then brought to a disposal facility.

Oblena warned the public of the adverse effects of hot meat, explaining that side effects included stomachaches, headaches, vomiting, and defecating. Those who consume the mishandled meat could be hospitalized, he added. -- Jeanella P. Manglapuz/BAP, GMA News

title: Some good in spite of...

After a week of incessant rains I was wondering if any good would come out of the storms, habagat and tropical depressions that seemed to park themselves in the Philippine area of responsibility.

The only "good" I could think of that may come out of the rains, particularly the widespread flooding all over northern and southern Luzon, was it would serve as a cold and brutal reminder, if not a wake-up call, that NO ONE, no CongTractor or elected official has been charged or landed in jail for the ghost flood control projects.

"So, sana ho ayusin na ho natin ang mga desisyon natin sa 2028, para hindi na po nakakaranas ng ganitong klaseng inconvenience 'yung mga kababayan ho natin na nakakaranas po ng pagbaha at siyempre nangangailangang lumikas sa panahon po ng habagat o ng bagyo at tuloy-tuloy na pag-ulan," she said.

title: Need for emergency feeding of children, part 2
content_lead:
The Philippine government has several programs to combat child undernutrition. The two largest are the Supplementary Feeding Program (SFP) of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and the School-Based Feeding Program (SBFP) of the Department of Education (DepEd). The SFP targets children three to five years old enrolled in Child Development Centers (daycare centers) and Supervised Neighborhood Play groups.

The program provides daily nutritious hot meals (and, in some areas, milk) for 180 feeding days in 2026. It includes nutrition education for parents and caregivers, along with regular monitoring of the children’s weight and nutritional status. Local government units (LGUs) get involved under the Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act. This year, the DSWD expanded the program to serve more than 1.8 million children nationwide, backed by a larger budget and a longer feeding period.

DepEd’s School-Based Feeding Program focuses on public school learners, especially those identified as wasted, severely wasted, or otherwise nutritionally at-risk. The program provides daily nutritious meals during the school year, milk feeding in many schools, and regular health and nutrition assessments. On July 8, 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced the nationwide expansion of the school feeding program, stating that the government intends to broaden coverage so that more learners receive nutritious meals while also supporting the Filipino farmers who supply the food. True enough, this program was given prominence in his State of the Nation Address (SONA) yesterday.

The government also supports child nutrition through the National Nutrition Council and the Philippine Plan of Action for Nutrition. Maternal and child nutrition services of the Department of Health include breastfeeding promotion, micronutrient supplementation, growth monitoring, deworming, and nutrition counseling. Additionally, local government units have their own community nutrition and food security initiatives. One of the most successful was implemented in Quezon Province when now-Congressman Jay Suarez was governor. Quezon Province was one of the pioneers in implementing the First 1,000 Days program, feeding the baby even while still in the womb of the mother.

Because of the magnitude of this problem of child stunting due to undernutrition, the private sector must do its share in ensuring that vulnerable children receive adequate nourishment during their critical years of growth and learning. That is why the Philippine Food Bank Foundation decided to partner with a public school in Muntinlupa in a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) program called “Balik Lusog.”

It was launched at Poblacion Elementary School in Muntinlupa in partnership with the Loaves and Fish Foundation, made possible by a generous grant from the Starbucks Foundation. The children that the program set out to feed were 500 learners from Grades 3 to 6—children identified as malnourished or undernourished. Many of them come from families relocated from the railroad tracks. They were coming to school on empty stomachs, and because they were hungry, it was very difficult for them to learn.

For 38 school days—from Jan. 26 to March 19, 2026—the Loaves and Fish kitchen cooked fresh, nutritious meals every single morning. Parent volunteers from a private school, PAREF Southridge, delivered the meals to the school. Teachers and the school nurse watched over every child every single school day. At the end of those 38 days, the children were subjected to health measurements: ninety-five percent (95 percent) of the 500 children gained weight. Furthermore, every subject—English, Filipino, Science, Mathematics, and Araling Panlipunan—showed higher test scores in the fourth quarter than in the quarter prior to when the feeding started.

Children who used to arrive tired and distracted became more alert. Children with frequent absences started showing up daily—because for some of them, the meal served in school was the only decent meal for the whole day. One child told a teacher, “I am excited to come to school now.” That child, fed, healthy, and learning today, is the nurse, the engineer, the teacher, or the entrepreneur of tomorrow. The Philippine Food Bank spent just 57 centavos per meal to invest in the human resources of tomorrow, thanks to the donation of surplus food, dedicated volunteers, and the quiet faith of sponsors who agreed to help even before they knew the outcome.

Fortunately, the Starbucks Foundation has generously invited the Philippine Food Bank to apply for a second grant. The officials, with the support of numerous donors—among them those who participated in the Golf Tournament at Tagaytay Midlands—have every intention of going beyond one grant and one school. The Balik Lusog program resumed at Poblacion Elementary School in Muntinlupa on July 27, 2026, the exact same day that President Marcos delivered his SONA. Close to 1,000 undernourished children in Grades two to six will once again be fed for as many days as possible during the school year.

From there, the Foundation plans to bring Balik Lusog to every public elementary school in Muntinlupa, hopefully in partnership with the School-Based Feeding Program of the Department of Education. The Foundation is now in conversations with officials from the Department of Education so that a formal Public-Private Partnership framework can be developed on the basis of our experience at the elementary school in Muntinlupa. Our next target is the City of Pasig, where two leading government officials, Mayor Vico Sotto and Congressman Roman Romulo, are among the most enlightened on this long-festering problem of child undernutrition and its very deleterious effect on the quality of our human resources.

After the Foundation perfects the Muntinlupa and Pasig models, there is no limit to what can be accomplished across the numerous Philippine municipalities. We hope the Balik Lusog experiment in Muntinlupa can inspire other private initiatives combating hunger in the Philippines to adopt the PPP model, ensuring government funds are best utilized with a minimum of inefficiency and poor governance.

I am especially referring to several notable private initiatives. Among corporate foundation feeding programs, many large Philippine enterprises operate long-term nutrition programs through their foundations, including the Jollibee Group Foundation (Busog, Lusog, Talino—BLT—feeding program and community kitchens), Pilipinas Shell Foundation (school-community nutrition projects), Ayala Foundation (nutrition and maternal-child health initiatives), Aboitiz Foundation (community feeding and nutrition education), Metrobank Foundation (support for nutrition and health programs), Manila Water Foundation (nutrition linked to clean water and sanitation), ABS-CBN Lingkod Kapamilya Foundation (feeding and nutrition assistance), and GMA Kapuso Foundation (nutrition and disaster feeding).

Faith-based organizations also play a vital role, including Caritas Philippines, Feed the Hungry Philippines, various Catholic diocesan feeding programs, and several Protestant and Evangelical feeding groups. Similarly, NGO-led nutrition programs contribute immensely to the cause, such as the Philippine Food Bank Foundation, Rise Against Hunger, Project PEARLS, Kabisig ng Kalahi, Gawad Kalinga, and the NVC Foundation, whose Mingo nutrition program provides fortified complementary food to undernourished children.

I have by no means prepared an exhaustive list of private initiatives that directly address the serious problem of undernourished children. In fact, it can be arguably stated that the Philippines has one of Southeast Asia’s broadest networks of private-sector nutrition initiatives. Corporate foundations, NGOs, churches, civic organizations, and international partners collectively invest hundreds of millions of pesos each year in feeding programs, nutrition, food fortification, community kitchens, breastfeeding promotion, and livelihood initiatives.

content_lead:
THE Climate Change Commission (CCC) on Thursday stressed the need to provide a blueprint for context-specific climate-resilient policies at the 2026 National Climate Resilience Forum.

The forum, held on Thursday in Taguig City, convened local leaders to advance the National Adaptation Plan which outlines how a country will adapt to the long-term climate impacts.

"National frameworks provide a coherent road map for enhancing climate resilience as we pursue low-carbon development. However, we know that policies on paper cannot protect a community from a storm, and it is only through decisive action on the ground," said CCC Commissioner Rachel Anne Herrera.

To achieve this requires risk-sensitive and localized planning to address specific vulnerabilities, Herrera said.

Robert Borje, CCC vice chairman and executive director, said adaptation "can't remain an aspiration of any group; it must become visible in safer schools and cities, stronger infrastructure, protected coastlines, climate-smart agriculture and forward local governance." "Over the past months, our committee has been actively deliberating measures that seek to strengthen the country's climate governance and accelerate the transition toward a resilient and low-carbon economy," said Tolentino.

title: Promises, performance, and the 'mahiya naman kayo' moment

Last year's address was defined by bold commitments: ₱20 rice, zero-balance billing in hospitals, lifeline electricity rates, and expanded support for small businesses. Today, as we evaluate the administration's progress, the measure of this SONA will not be found in applause lines, but in whether performance has caught up with promise.

When President Marcos Jr. delivered his 2025 State of the Nation Address, he chose to speak less of promises and more of performance. It was a deliberate pivot: a leader entering the final stretch of his term, conscious that history will judge him not by rhetoric but by delivery.

However, the numbers in 2026 tell a more complex story than the optimism of a year ago. While the 2025 address offered hope, the current economic landscape faces significant headwinds. Inflation, which had tempered to 1.4 percent by June 2025, has proven stubborn, rising to 6.4 percent in June 2026. This remains consistently above the central bank's 2-4 percent target, keeping the cost of living high for ordinary families. Furthermore, core inflation -- which strips away volatile items -- reached 4.4 percent in June, the highest in 31 months, signaling that price pressures have become broad-based.

"Ipinagbibigay-alam sa publiko na ang lahat ng hiking activities sa Mt. Pico de Loro/ MPPMNGPL ay pansamantalang sususpindihin mula Agosto 21, 2026 - Setyembre 12, 2026, upang bigyang-daan ang paglilinis, pagsasaayos, at rehabilitasyon ng mga napinsalang bahagi ng pinangangalagaang pook dulot ng nagdaang bagyo at habagat," the advisory read.

The DENR said that it will conduct inspection and maintenance of hiking trails, clearing of fallen trees and other obstructions, as well as other necessary measures for the safety of the hikers.

The Mount Pico de Loro is part of the 3,972-hectare MPPMNGPL, along with other peaks: Palay-palay and Mataas-na-Gulod.

Pico de Loro was named for its summit that resembles a parrot's beak. It is also the highest mountain in Cavite at 2,257 feet.

title: Searca, Seameo partner for regenerative agri
content_lead:
LOS BAÑOS, Laguna -- The Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture (Searca) will lead the development of a regional micro-credential curriculum on regenerative and resilient agriculture in collaboration with two other centers under the Southeast Asian Ministers of Education Organization (Seameo).

The 12-month project, funded through the Seameo Inter-Centre Collaboration (ICC) Grant, will design and pilot test a competency-based curriculum for agricultural educators, technical-vocational trainers, extension workers, and early-career practitioners across the region.

SEARCA LOGO

The three institutions were selected in the first round of the ICC Grant, which supports joint programs addressing shared regional priorities.

Training on regenerative agriculture in Southeast Asia remains uneven, according to project documents. Many current opportunities are tied to short-term donor-funded projects or private sector programs. Universities, technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions, and extension agencies often lack structured materials that can be integrated into regular courses or continuing professional development.

title: Drones help develop better rice varieties
content_lead:
FOR years, making better rice meant scientists walking fields with clipboards and testing plants one by one. Now, researchers at the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) are doing much of that work from the sky -- and in the lab.

In a study published in Current Plant Biology, IRRI scientists used drones and genetic testing to find rice varieties that can turn sunlight into grain more efficiently. The goal is simple: grow more rice on the same land, even as the climate gets hotter and less predictable.

The study, "Diversity of photosynthesis-related and high-throughput phenotyping traits in indica rice," was led by Hsiang-Chun Lin, Jacqueline Dionora, Dmytro Chebotarov, Ma. Rebecca Laza, Ma. Elizabeth Naredo, Pauline Muyco, Stephen Klassen, Amelia Henry, W. Paul Quick, and Kenneth McNally.

Why this matters

By 2050, the world will need about 50 percent more rice and other grains to feed a growing population. But rice yields are only increasing by less than 1 percent each year.

title: Searca highlights climate-resilient farming, promising ube varieties
content_lead:
LOS BAÑOS, Laguna -- Long prized as a staple in Filipino culinary tradition, purple yam -- locally known as ube -- is emerging as a key driver of agricultural growth and climate resilience for smallholder farmers.

Insights featured in the Agriculture and Development Seminar Series (ADSS) organized by the Southeast Asian Regional Center for Graduate Study and Research in Agriculture (Searca) show that while global and domestic demand for ube continues to surge, local supply struggles to keep pace, creating a significant opportunity to transform traditional root-crop farming into a highly profitable enterprise.

Market demand remains strong, with ube exports generating $3.06 million in 2025 through sought-after processed products such as powders, purees, and traditional pastes (halaya).

However, domestic production reached only about 13,535 metric tons in 2022, compared with a national demand of 49,000 metric tons. Low baseline yields, seasonal crop behavior, tuber dormancy, and a shortage of quality planting materials continue to limit overall production.

To bridge this gap, agricultural frameworks under the High Value Crops Development Program (HVCDP) of the Department of Agriculture (DA) are prioritizing crop resilience and diversification.

title: În El Salvador a fost descoperit un mormînt vechi de aproape 3.000 de ani
content_lead:
Arheologii din El Salvador au descoperit un mormînt neobișnuit, vechi de 2.800 de ani.

Scheletul uman zăcea cu fața în jos, iar lîngă el s-a păstrat un vas de ceramică în formă de broască țestoasă marină, relatează "MIR24".

Mormîntul a fost descoperit pe 2 iulie într-o zonă suburbană a orașului San Salvador. Mormîntul se afla sub un strat de cenușă vulcanică provenită din erupția craterului Plan de la Laguna. Acest cataclism este datat între anii 850-830 î.Hr., adică în perioada clasică mijlocie din Mezoamerica.

Conform datelor furnizate de cercetători, în această perioadă, societățile din sud-estul Mezoamericii duceau un mod de viață mai sedentar, creau culturi mai complexe și dezvoltau agricultura. Se credea că practicau și sacrificii umane, dar, în ultima vreme, cercetătorii au început să pună la îndoială această concluzie.

Conform noii teorii, înmormîntările neobișnuite ar fi putut fi legate nu de sacrificii, ci de o concepție străveche despre cosmos și lumea subterană. Vasul ceramic în formă de broască țestoasă ar fi putut simboliza centura lui Orion.

În astronomia maya ulterioară, acesta apărea ca parte a unei călătorii sacre.

În continuare, cercetătorii vor efectua analize chimice ale scheletului. Acest lucru va permite aflarea mai multor detalii despre viața omului, dieta sa și posibila cauză a decesului. Cercetările vor dura aproximativ un an.

title: Why wetlands matter more than ever
content_lead:
"Wetlands are weird," said Dr. Jerome L. Montemayor, executive director of the Laguna-based ASEAN Centre for Biodiversity. "To those who are unfamiliar, it either looks like a muddy lake or a waterlogged forest. But after years in this field, you will definitely learn to appreciate these valuable natural resources and say that wetlands certainly have more than meets the eye."

Paul A. Keddy, author of "Wetland Ecology: Principles and Conservation," defines a wetland as "an ecosystem that arises when inundation by water produces soil dominated by anaerobic processes which, in turn, forces the biota, particularly rooted plants, to adapt to flooding."

A patch of land that develops pools of water after a rainstorm would not be considered a wetland, even though the land is wet. Specifically, wetlands are characterized by a water table that stands at or near the land surface for a prolonged period each year, allowing aquatic plants to thrive.

Wetlands are vital ecosystems in the country's natural environment. They are classified into three main types: freshwater, estuarine, and marine. These include natural wetlands such as rivers, lakes, swamps, marshes, peatlands, ponds, mangrove forests, seagrass meadows, and reef flats, as well as man-made wetlands such as dams and rice fields.

"As an archipelago, we are shaped by water," explained Robert E.A. Borje, Vice Chairperson and Executive Director of the Climate Change Commission, the country's lead policy-making body on climate change. "Mangroves line our coasts, wetlands sit at river mouths and floodplains, and inland marshes and lakes regulate rainfall and runoff."

According to Borje, these ecosystems serve as an initial barrier against concentrated climate hazards. They are where storm surges lose intensity, floodwaters spread instead of wreaking havoc, and risks are reduced before they escalate into disasters.

Laguna Lake, otherwise known as Laguna de Bay is now in its dying state and needs to be saved.

Fr. Reynante "Nante" Tolentino, shrine rector of the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of the Our Lady of the Holy Rosary (DSPOLHR) in Cardona, Rizal said on Tuesday, August 4, that the lake, considered as the largest fresh water lake in the country, is 'gasping for breath'.

In his homily during the Holy Mass held at Cardona Fish Port a day prior to the observance of the second anniversary of the consecration of Laguna de Bay on Aug. 5, Fr. Nante called on the local and national government agencies and their leaders to take immediate action to save the lake which he likened to a mother who is in a hospital's intensive care unit.

Tolentino, who is also the current president of the Association of Catholic Shrines and Pilgrimage of the Philippines (ACSP) told Manila Bulletin that his homily was meant to enlighten authorities in the government agencies that the death of the lake would eventually lead to starvation and even death as many families in the lakeshore municipalities in Laguna and Rizal depend on the lake's produce for livelihood.

The Cardona's Marian shrine rector's view on the condition of the lake is also shared by the shrine as it also posted a comment entitled, "Ang Lawa ay Umiiyak, Nakikinig Ba Tayo?" (The Lake is Crying. Are We Listening?"

Tolentino issued his view in time for the commemoration this year of the second anniversary of the lake's consecration by Antipolo Bishop Ruperto Santos, when on Aug. 5, 2024, the bishop offered prayers and blessed the lake a year after the Laguna Lake drowning incident happened in 2023 that killed 27 people.

The lake is surrounded by several municipalities in Rizal-the municipalities of Cardona, Binangonan, Angono, Baras, Tanay, Pililla, and Jalajala and 17 localities in Laguna Province, and Muntinlupa, Taguig and Pateros in Metro Manila.

title: High tides to cause flooding in San Diego coastal areas
content_lead:
SAN DIEGO (FOX 5/KUSI) -- All of San Diego County's 70-mile coastline is under a flood advisory to start the week as high tides are expected.

The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a Coastal Flood Advisory for San Diego and Orange County coastal areas from 6 p.m. Monday to 11 p.m. Wednesday for high tides of 7.2 to 7.5-feet.

The high tides will peak between 7:30 p.m. and 10 p.m. due to astronomical high tides.

During the advisory, coastal areas can expect flooding in low-lying parking lots, parks and roads, NWS says. Some coastal roads may be closed due to flooding; do not drive around barricades or through water if you don't know how deep it is. It is also advised to take precautions to protect any flood-prone property.

At Tamarack Beach in Carlsbad, a portion of the parking lot is closed and crumbling and much of the sand on the beach was washed away after four recent major south swells caused significant erosion.

The high tides caused Metrolink to temporarily suspend Orange County Line service between the Laguna Niguel/Mission Viejo and Oceanside stations through Friday, Aug. 14.

Metrolink said the suspension was put in place as a precaution after similar high-tide conditions late last month caused significant delays.

At this time, the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner will continue its normal routes as long as it is safe, according to Metrolink.

High temperatures across the county are forecast to slowly lower this week before they reach near to slightly below average temperatures on Wednesday, according to NWS.

Humidity is currently in the high 60s.

At the same time, a chance of thunderstorms will stick around Monday and Tuesday in the mountain and desert areas.

title: Laguna Bluebelt's photo contest displays local ocean beauty
content_lead:
Stunning images that celebrate the diversity of wildlife and ocean habitat found along Laguna Beach's protected shoreline are on display for a limited time.

The Laguna Bluebelt Coalition recently recognized amateur and professional photographers in its 15th annual Bluebelt Photo Contest. The event held at the LCAD Gallery along Ocean Avenue awarded prizes to photographers in several categories. Their photos are on display through Aug. 16.

The purpose of the contest is to recognize and celebrate the natural wonders off the Laguna Beach coastline, with a special emphasis on the Marine Protected Areas, which are designated beaches, coves and rock outcroppings along five miles of the town where no wildlife, rock, shell, crustacean, or fish can be touched or removed.

"The photo contest documents the animals and the habitat that's in the Marine Protected Areas," said Anne Girtz, a civil engineer and member of the Bluebelt Coalition. "It's this citizen scientist and documentation of the value and the diversity of critters that are in (the MPA) areas."

This year's winning photographers include Jordan Manning, of Dana Point, who received first place in the professional category with a photo capturing a moment beneath the kelp where he encountered a curious harbor seal.

Manning said he photographed the harbor seal, known as "Waffles," which has gained national attention for her friendliness toward divers, in November.

He said the protections along so much of the city's shoreline make it unique and "because of that, it allows the animals to thrive and flourish rather than having to worry about people running around the kelp with spear guns or taking their fish. They know we're just there to observe and not going to harm them.

"She sees people, and she just comes straight up," he added, "zero fear in her eyes."

title: The Number-1 Food to Lower Blood Pressure, According to Cardiologists
content_lead:
What you eat plays a powerful role in your blood pressure and heart health overall. Incorporating the number-one food to lower blood pressure into your diet on a regular basis is one of the simplest things you can do to lower blood pressure naturally.

Meet the experts: Cheng-Han Chen, M.D., an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA; Kevin Kheder, M.D., an interventional cardiologist at Hoag's Jeffrey M. Carlton Heart & Vascular Institute in Newport Beach, CA.

"There isn't a single 'magic' food that will lower your blood pressure overnight," says Cheng-Han Chen, M.D., an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA. "Instead, long-term control comes from building a balanced, heart-healthy eating pattern. Focus on filling your plate with plenty of fruits and vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains." Adopting an eating plan like the Mediterranean diet or the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet is a smart strategy for keeping your blood pressure at a healthy level.

Still, some foods certainly help support healthy blood pressure better than others. "If I had to choose one food, I'd recommend legumes -- black beans, lentils, or chickpeas," says Kevin Kheder, M.D., an interventional cardiologist at Hoag's Jeffrey M. Carlton Heart & Vascular Institute in Newport Beach, CA. "They are rich in potassium, magnesium, and fiber, which helps support healthy blood pressure. title: Coffee and agroforestry: A deliciously profitable mix
content_lead:
What's it like farming in a protected area? Agroforestry farmers Cristina Digo and Evelyn Buendia share their story.

The women live in Brgy. Himbubulo Weste in Guinayangan, Quezon. The protected area is located in Mulawin Spring and is part of an Area of Multi-Use Zone under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources' (DENR). "You're not allowed to cut trees, but you're allowed to plant them," Cristina said. "If you cut one tree, you have to replace it with 50."

I am here on the invitation of Dr. Julian Gonsalves, Senior Asia Program Advisor at the International Institute for Rural Reconstruction (IIRR), an international organization focusing on rural development.

The women are recipients of IIRR and the Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research's (CGIAR) ClimBeR project, a climate resilience project, which, in this case, involves giving coffee and other fruit seedlings to target beneficiaries to aid coffee production. The resulting crops are processed and sold to local cooperatives like Asosasyon ng Responsableng Magkakape (AROMA) and Guinayangan Coffee Agri-Farmers, Processors, and Entrepreneurs Agriculture Cooperative (GCAFPEA). The interview was conducted in Tagalog.

The seedlings are intercropped under existing coconut trees, with recipients receiving 100-500 seedlings, depending on their land area. The program also provides local fruit seedlings like guyabano, lanzones, rambutan, mangoes, mangosetten, and durian, usually around 10-20 seedlings per variety.

Program coordinator Roel Jordan explained that recipients undergo an orientation on proper cultivation before receiving the seedlings. Harvests are sold at the local market and sometimes through private buyers as well.

Cristina, who is also the local AROMA president, is 58 years old and has been farming for 30 years. Though, like much of Quezon, intercropping her coconut trees with robusta coffee, guyabano, rambutan, lanzones, bananas, durian, and mangosteen.

title: Marcos distributes cash aid to Lucena scholars
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. handed out cash assistance to 165 presidential scholars currently enrolled in private colleges in this city on Tuesday here at the Lucena Convention Center.

Each student received a one-time P20,000 educational assistance under the Bagong Pilipinas Barangay Presidential Scholars Program.

Marcos said this grassroot project is aimed at strengthening the education capability of students and to curb the increasing number of learners who are forced to stop schooling due to lack of financial support.

"This privilege is funded by the Local Government Support Fund, enabling all local government units to provide adequate education opportunities to our young residents," Marcos said.

The program is a national government initiative where each barangay may have five scholars.

Marcos also led the distribution of a 10-kilo sack of rice for each of the 52,400 indigent households in Lucena under the "Bigay Bigas sa Masa" initiative.

The rice distribution is part of the Sagip Saka Act with the government directly buying harvested rice from local farmers and distributing it to vulnerable sectors.

Also present during the distribution were Lucena Mayor Mark Alcala, Quezon Gov. Helen Tan and Vice Gov. Anacleto Alcala III.

Marcos also led the distribution of the Certificate of Entitlement under Presidential Proclamation 436, Series of 2003, that provides urban poor families and city government employees their own parcel of land in Barangay Ibabang Iyam, a 17.6-hectare property previously owned by the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines.

title: PBBM brings 'Bawat Bayan Makikinabang' program in Lucena City

President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Tuesday led the "Bawat Bayan Makikinabang" program in Lucena City, Quezon, highlighting the administration's commitment to ensuring that government programs reach communities across the country through strengthened support to local government units (LGUs).

title: Coconut agency promotes husk amid El Niño drought
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- Amid the extreme heat and water shortages brought by the El Niño phenomenon, the Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA) is encouraging farmers to adopt a simple but effective practice to help protect trees and crops: coconut husk mulching.

"One simple yet effective method to help keep trees healthy is the use of coconut husk (bunot ng niyog) as mulch around the base of trees," the PCA offices for Laguna and Rizal said in a Facebook post.

According to the agency, coconut husk mulch helps retain soil moisture by reducing the rapid evaporation of water, especially during periods of intense heat and prolonged dry conditions.

READ: INQToday: Signal No. 2 up as Tropical Storm Kiyapo moves closer to PH

The practice also protects plant roots by acting as a natural insulator against high soil temperatures. It helps suppress weed growth by reducing competition for water and nutrients needed by crops.

"[It] improves soil quality. As coconut husk decomposes, it adds organic matter that enhances soil structure and fertility," the PCA said.

The agency added that coconut husk mulching can also help conserve irrigation water because soil moisture lasts longer, reducing the need for frequent watering.

Aside from being practical and affordable, the method is also environmentally friendly since coconut husks - often treated as agricultural waste - can be reused as a natural protective layer for plants.

"With every coconut husk used as mulch, we help maintain the health of our trees and strengthen their ability to withstand the impacts of El Niño," the PCA said.

The agency urged farmers and coconut growers to adopt eco-friendly farming practices and proper plantation management to improve the resilience of farms against climate-related challenges. INQ

title: Farmers' group calls for genuine agrarian reform ahead of Sona
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY, Quezon - A national peasant organization urged President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. to go beyond calls for unity and translate his commitments into concrete measures to address the continuing struggles of Filipino farmers as he delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27.

"The true measure of this administration will not be the promises it makes from the podium, but whether it finally delivers justice, security, and dignity to agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs) and all those who feed the nation," The Kilusan Para sa Tunay na Repormang Agraryo at Katarungang Panlipunan (Katarungan) said in a recent statement.

The group stressed that without genuine agrarian reform and social justice, government commitments would remain beyond the reach of the very farmers whose labor sustains the country.

Katarungan recalled that during Marcos' fourth SONA following the 2025 midterm elections, he appealed to government officials to set aside political differences and focus on their common responsibility of serving the Filipino people.

The organization noted that Marcos had acknowledged public dissatisfaction over the government's delivery of basic services despite reported economic gains.

The President also vowed that the remaining years of his administration would focus on improving the lives of Filipinos and fulfilling his government's commitments.

"One year later, these commitments must be judged not by rhetoric, but by results," Katarungan said.

The group said the administration's commitment to farmers should be measured by how effectively it protects, completes, and implements agrarian reform while improving the conditions of rural communities.

"For millions of ARBs and farmers, dignity cannot be measured by speeches or symbolism," the organization said.

Instead, Katarungan said dignity means having secure and undisputed rights to the land they cultivate, protection against land grabbing and displacement, full use of awarded land

title: DAR distributes P5.49M in farm machinery to Calabarzon beneficiaries
content_lead:
THE Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) on Sunday said it distributed P5.49 million worth of farm machinery and equipment to beneficiaries and farmer organizations in the provinces of Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Quezon (Calabarzon).

DAR Undersecretary for Field Operations Kazel Celeste led the turnover on July 21 in Lucena. The distribution was part of DAR's agrarian reform program, which also included the awarding of certificates of land ownership, certificates of condonation and release of mortgage, and electronic titles under the Support to Parcelization of Lands for Individual Titling project.

Batangas received P1.98 million worth of equipment, including a 40-horsepower, four-wheel-drive tractor with rotary tiller and disc plow, three motorcycles with carriers, weighing scales and powered pressure washers.

Cavite got a 50-horsepower, four-wheel tractor worth P1.47 million.

Quezon I was given a motorcycle with sidecar and a hand tractor worth P300,000, while Quezon II received a multi-tiller, ride-on mini combine harvester, mechanical rice transplanter, grass cutters and knapsack sprayers worth P1.75 million.

title: 70 families evacuated as rains batter Taytay, Rizal
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - Residents of low-lying and flood-prone areas in Taytay, Rizal were enjoined by the municipal government on Saturday to take immediate safety measures amid continuous rains triggered by the southwest monsoon or "habagat."

As of 1 p.m., at least 70 families, or 240 individuals, from the barangays of Muzon, Dolores and San Juan were evacuated and were temporarily staying at evacuation centers, the municipal Public Information Office (PIO) said.

"Do not wait for the situation to worsen before evacuating. Put the safety of your family first, especially children, senior citizens, pregnant women, persons with disabilities (PWDs), and those with medical conditions," the municipal PIO said in an advisory in Filipino.

The municipal government continues to monitor the situation and prepare for the safety of residents affected by the persistent rains and rising water levels.

The Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO), together with other concerned municipal offices, are closely monitoring conditions in various areas and remains on standby to respond to the needs of affected residents.

Authorities reminded residents to remain alert, follow official advisories, and evacuate early if conditions in their areas become unsafe.

title: 'Habagat' rains affect 3,640 families in Rizal, Cavite, Batangas
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY, Philippines - Heavy rains brought by Tropical Depression Maymay and the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, have affected 3,640 families in the provinces of Rizal, Cavite, and Batangas, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Sunday, Aug.9.

"Based on the reports received by the field office from affected local government units, there are already 3,640 affected families in 50 barangays in the provinces of Rizal, Cavite and Batangas," the DSWD Calabarzon Field Office said in a report Sunday noon.

More than 400 of the affected families were staying in 27 evacuation centers opened and managed by their respective local government units (LGUs), the agency added.

READ: Habagat brings heavy rains, flooding in parts of PH

The DSWD field office continued to monitor the effects of the southwest monsoon and Maymay across the Calabarzon Region.

Maymay had dissipated into a low-pressure area and exited the Philippine Area of Responsibility on Friday, along with Typhoon Dolphin. However, the southwest monsoon continued to bring rains over parts of Luzon.

The DSWD said its field offices throughout the region were ready to provide disaster-response augmentation to affected LGUs, while provincial, city, and municipal quick response teams had remained on standby since Aug. 5.

As of August 6, DSWD Calabarzon had strategically prepositioned 227,216 family food packs worth P148.27 million, 11,630 ready-to-eat food packs worth P8.88 million, and 11,119 non-food items worth P21.57 million in 78 warehouses across the region.

The field office also had P3 million in standby funds to facilitate the immediate procurement of additional relief goods and other essential resources should the need arise.

The DSWD urged affected LGUs and communities to remain vigilant and continue coordinating with disaster response authorities as weather conditions develop. /atm

title: Laguna extends school suspensions to Tuesday as monsoon
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - Laguna Governor Sol Aragones has extended the suspension of face-to-face classes at all levels throughout the province to Tuesday, Aug. 11, as heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon continue to pound the Calabarzon region.

"Children, our province is still experiencing moderate to heavy rains, with flooding reported in some areas and some residents continuing to stay in evacuation centers," Aragones appeared to address pupils in a Facebook post in Filipino at 7:30 p.m. Monday (August 10).

"To ensure the safety of our students, we have decided to suspend classes again throughout the province of Laguna," she added.

READ: Walang pasok: Class, work suspensions on Aug. 11

Schools will employ alternative learning protocols while face-to-face classes remain suspended, Aragones instructed.

The governor had initially cancelled school activities on Monday because of the bad weather.

In a message posted Sunday night, Aragones cited continuing rains, strong winds, flooding and the more than 3,000 residents who had been staying in evacuation centers.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) forecast that heavy rains associated with the enhanced southwest monsoon would continue until Wednesday (August 12), although rainfall was expected to gradually weaken beginning Tuesday.

title: 96 families flee flooding as heavy rains batter Lian in Batangas
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- The number of residents evacuating at Lian town in Batangas, continued to rise Tuesday (August 18) as relentless rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon triggered flooding in several areas of the town.

"Based on the status of open evacuation centers report of the Municipal Social Welfare and Development Office (MSWDO) for the southwest monsoon, a total of 96 families, or 318 individuals, are currently staying in the evacuation centers," the municipal government said in a report on Tuesday afternoon.

READ: 28 Cavite, Batangas towns, cities suspend classes due to rains

As of noon, the displaced residents were being sheltered in 11 schools, barangay halls and chapels that had been opened as evacuation centers.

The municipal government also reported that a fishing boat was used to evacuate residents who needed to leave flood-hit areas in Barangay San Diego.

Floodwaters in the area have risen up to chest level along a portion of the road, making passage difficult and prompting authorities to assist residents in affected communities.

Lian remained under a red rainfall warning due to continued heavy rains, according to the state weather bureau.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) uses a three-level, color-coded rainfall warning system -- yellow, orange and red -- to indicate the intensity and potential danger of heavy rainfall.

Red is the highest and most dangerous warning level, indicating intense rainfall that may cause serious flooding and landslides.

Under the red warning category, rainfall of 30 millimeters or more within an hour is expected, prompting authorities and residents in affected areas to take immediate action. /jpv

title: 2,947 families displaced as habagat continues to batter Calabarzon
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY -- The number of families temporarily displaced from their homes across the Calabarzon region has risen as heavy rains from the enhanced southwest monsoon, or habagat, continued to trigger flooding in parts of the region, the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) reported on Thursday.

"Based on reports from affected local governments, 138 evacuation centers are currently open, serving 2,947 families," the DSWD in Region IV-A said in its latest report.

Most of the displaced families were from Batangas, the DSWD said.

READ: Pagasa sees improving weather on Thursday as Neneng, habagat weaken

The agency also reported that 265,628 families from 914 barangays across Cavite, Laguna, Batangas, Rizal, and Quezon provinces have been affected by persistent heavy rains as of Aug. 19.

The figure was significantly higher than the 218,986 affected families in 844 barangays as of Aug. 18.

Of the 138 operational evacuation centers, the agency's Aug. 19 tally was topped by Batangas with 63, followed by Rizal with 36, Quezon with 18, Laguna with 16, and Cavite with five.

Only 21 evacuation centers across Calabarzon were operational on Aug. 18.

As part of its continued relief operations, the DSWD regional office has provided P128.9 million worth of assistance to affected families in the region as of Aug. 19. This included the distribution of 204,495 family food packs.

A standard DSWD family food pack contains six kilograms of rice, canned goods such as corned beef, tuna, and sardines, and sachets of coffee or chocolate malt drink. It is designed to provide a family of five with food for two days.

The agency said assistance was extended not only to families who evacuated but also to those who remained in their homes but were affected by the rains and flooding./coa

title: Quezon priest challenges Marcos' agrarian reform claims in Sona
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - A Catholic priest serving in Quezon province is contesting President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s claims of success in implementing agrarian reform, saying the continuing plight of farmers in Sariaya town tells a different story.

"If agrarian reform has truly been successful, why do farmers in Sariaya who have already been awarded Certificates of Land Ownership Award (CLOAs) and have cultivated their land for many years remain at risk of losing it?" Fr. Warren Puno, director of the Ministry of Ecology of the Diocese of Lucena, said in response to the President's July 27 State of the Nation Address (SONA).

In his SONA, President Marcos said the government had distributed more than 400,000 land titles covering over 500,000 hectares during the past four years.

READ: Marcos vows to complete land title distribution in 2027

"The reality experienced by farmers in Sariaya is far removed from the picture of success being portrayed," the Quezon priest said.

Puno also urged Agrarian Reform Secretary Conrado Estrella III to remain in office and continue leading the Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR).

Puno argued that land distribution alone does not constitute genuine agrarian reform.

"Land distribution alone is not enough if the land cannot be protected," he said in a statement. "Genuine agrarian reform is not merely about issuing land titles. It is about steadfastly defending the rights of beneficiaries against any attempt to reclaim the land they have cultivated and developed for many years," the priest said.

Puno reiterated Sariaya farmers' appeal for Marcos to immediately address their long-standing grievances and ensure that justice is served.

The dispute involves 522 hectares of agricultural land spanning four barangays in Sariaya. Between 1989 and 1992, about 328.877 hectares were distributed to 266 agrarian reform beneficiaries under the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program (CARP).

title: Venomous Philippine cobra rescued inside duck pen in Tayabas City
content_lead:
LUCENA CITY - A venomous Philippine cobra was rescued after it was found inside a duck pen in Tayabas City, Quezon, on Monday morning.

The serpent was safely captured at around 11 a.m. in Barangay Ilasan Ilaya by a team from the Tayabas City Environment and Natural Resources Office (CENRO) led by its chief, Melvin Rada.

Photos of the rescue show the cobra had been hidden inside one of the wooden posts of the duck pen.

READ: Girl dies after shielding 3 cousins from cobra attack in Sarangani

After it was secured, the snake was placed inside a plastic box and was turned over to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources' Community Environment and Natural Resources Office (DENR-CENRO) for proper assessment and disposition.

"Although the Philippine cobra is highly venomous, it generally poses no threat to humans unless it is disturbed, provoked, or threatened," the CENRO said in Filipino.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) classifies the Philippine cobra as a "near threatened" species. It is known to inhabit various environments, including tropical moist forests, agricultural areas, and urban communities.

A species listed as near threatened is considered at risk of becoming endangered if its population declines.

title: Indigenous community sees brighter future with solar energy
content_lead:
For most of her life, Liezel Sarmiento has lived without electricity.

Liezel is a member of Dumagat-Remontado tribe in Sitio Cablao, Pagsangahan, Gen. Nakar, Quezon province. Like everybody else in her mountain community she has to stop whatever she is doing when the sun begins to set.

Tribesmen usually travel for hours on rugged terrain to sell their produce and buy groceries in town. And there is not much they can do when they come home because it is already dark by that time. Chores have to wait for tomorrow.

Now, life in the community is changing for the better.

In celebration of its 50th Anniversary, BDO Unibank has stepped in to make life better in the Dumagat-Remontado community.

title: UPLIFT beneficiaries allocate cash aid for food, medicine, home repairs
content_lead:
Beneficiaries of the UPLIFT cash aid program said the money would go to food, medicine, and home repairs.

Beneficiaries of the government's expanded Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (UPLIFT) program began claiming their cash aid on Monday, saying they will spend it on daily necessities and house repairs in preparation for the rainy season.

In Oscar Oida's "24 Oras" report, the cash aid distribution, spearheaded by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), was simultaneously held across the country.

In Muntinlupa City, Luzviminda Gemina, 68, said that qualifying as a UPLIFT beneficiary was an "answered prayer," because she can finally fix their house, especially their roof that is full of holes.

"Nagulat na nga lang ako eh sa tagal ng panahon, ngayon lang ako nakatanggap. Nakatanggap man ako, sir, e bigas sa senior. Sakto po na makabili akong yero, kahit tatlo lang muna kasi ang kailangan na yero sa bahay ko, anim," Gemina said.

(I was surprised because this is the first time I've received something like this. Before, I only received the rice allowance for seniors. This is just in time for me to buy roofing sheets -- even just three for now, because my house actually needs six.)

Around 43 beneficiaries from Muntinlupa City received their P2,000 cash assistance on Monday. They were the only ones who showed up out of the 124 individuals who qualified in the program based on the Philippine Statistics Authority's 2024 community-based monitoring system.

title: Siblings cooking lunch killed in Rizal rockslide
content_lead:
Two siblings, aged 22 and 20, were killed after a boulder struck them while they were cooking lunch at the store where they worked during a rockslide in Sitio Wawa, Barangay San Rafael, Rodriguez, Rizal, on Wednesday, Aug. 5.

On Thursday, Aug. 6, Barangay Captain Judith Cruz told the Manila Bulletin that the siblings were with the 22-year-old female victim's husband before the incident. He had briefly left to fish near the store when the rockslide occurred around 12 p.m.

"Nangyari po yung incident doon sa tindahan po yun na kanilang pinag t-trabahuan. Nung 12, nagluluto yung magkapatid para sa tanghalian nila (The incident happened at the store where they worked. At around noon, the siblings were cooking their lunch when the incident occurred)," she said.

Cruz said the impact of the falling boulder was so strong that it hurled the female victim's body into the river, while her brother allegedly sustained fatal injuries.

She added that the boulder may have fallen from higher up, as there were reportedly no sounds of falling rocks before the incident. Only a single boulder was reported to have fallen.

"Walang narinig na parang nag-slide na bato, parang biglang deretso bagsak. So big sabihin (baka) ang taas ng pinanggalingan (There were no sounds of rocks sliding. It was as if the boulder suddenly fell straight down, so it may have come from much higher up)," she said.

Only the store where the victims were working at the time of the incident was affected by the falling boulder.

Cruz said the victims had also survived a rockslide last year, during which a boulder struck their home, although all members of the family escaped unharmed. She added that they had been advised to relocate from the area, but still went to Sitio Wawa for work.

She said she was saddened by the incident, noting that she had personally met and spoken with the female victim only recently, who was among those who received school supplies and rice from the barangay.

title: Philippines: The Upwelling Wind - ICSF
content_lead:
Fishers are bringing the NPOA-SSF to life through local leadership, collective ownership and community action

This article is by Ronald B. Rodriguez (rrodriguez.icsf@gmail.com), Asia Region Programme Officer, ICSF, The Philippines

Over a decade removed from the adoption of the Voluntary Guidelines for Securing Sustainable Small-Scale Fisheries in the Context of Food Security and Poverty Eradication (SSF Guidelines, 2014), the Philippine small-scale fisheries (SSF) subsector stands at a critical juncture. The creation of the SSF Guidelines involved about 4,000 stakeholders from civil society groups in 120 countries in the UN FAO-led process to ensure that the voices, concerns and rights of actual fishers and fishworkers were embedded in the final document. Following the endorsement of the SSF Guidelines, The Philippines became in 2024 the first country in Asia to develop a National Plan of Action for Small-Scale Fisheries (NPOA-SSF). The NPOA-SSF, rooted in the SSF Guidelines, has evolved into a national instrument designed to address the specific vulnerabilities and aspirations of the country's small-scale fisheries.

In November 2025, a capacity-building workshop organized by Tambuyog Development Center, Inc. (Tambuyog), with the support of ICSF, signalled a momentous shift in sectoral governance strategy: rather than waiting for top-down directives, fisherfolk networks and local stakeholders resolved to take ownership of the NPOA-SSF to ensure it becomes a living document that genuinely serves fisherfolk communities.

Translating strategic ownership of a process into practice necessitates navigating the complex governance and socio-economic realities of the Philippine SSF subsector. Six years after Typhoon Ulyses struck Montalban, Thelma found herself reliving the trauma as the recent rains brought back memories of the devastating floods.

With no available transportation, Thelma immediately carried her grandchild to safety and evacuated with her six grandchildren.

"I didn't know where my grandchildren could get a ride because the water suddenly rose. I had to make sacrifices to make sure my grandchildren would be safe," she said.

Thelma hopes that her community will no longer experience severe flooding and called for improvements to the area's drainage system.

"Hopefully, the flooding in our area can be prevented. I hope the drainage systems can be fixed because some of them are still clogged."

title: Budget release rate hits 88% at end-June
content_lead:
THE Department of Budget and Management (DBM) said it released 87.9% of the budget for 2026 as of the end of June.

According to the DBM Status of Allotment Release report, the releases amounted to P5.97 trillion out of the original budget total of P6.79 trillion, leaving P819.49 billion undistributed.

The release rate at the end of last month was running behind the year-earlier pace of 90%.

Releases to government agencies and departments amounted to P3.34 trillion by the end of June, equivalent to 90.9% of their allocations, compared to 94% in the same period last year.

Special-purpose funds released by the end of the month stood at P477 billion, representing 66.3% of the total allotment.

Meanwhile, automatic appropriation releases were at 89.8%, or P2.15 trillion.

These include the National Tax Allotment of P1.19 trillion, the P712.5 billion in interest payments, the P93.98 billion for the Block Grant, the P82.92 billion for retirement and life insurance premiums, and the P36.47 billion for a special account in the general fund, which includes the P6 billion allotment for the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement program.

"Other" releases amounted to P134.84 billion, which include continuing appropriations from last year worth P22.76 billion, P85.65 billion in unprogrammed appropriations, and other automatic appropriations worth P26.43 billion.

title: DoST pushes urban farming technologies to strengthen Metro Manila food security
content_lead:
The Department of Science and Technology (DoST) on Thursday said it is offering several urban farming technologies that can be adopted in Metro Manila to help strengthen the region's food security.

DoST Secretary Renato U. Solidum Jr. said smart agriculture is not limited to large agricultural lands but can also be implemented in urban areas through greenhouse farming for high-value crops, vertical farming, and aquaculture, even with limited space and materials.

He said these smart farming methods can be adopted by communities as well as individual households.

"They can grow a wide variety of vegetables and even crayfish using drums. These technologies can be introduced even in your own home," Mr. Solidum said during a press conference of the National Capital Region's (NCR) Regional Science, Technology, and Innovation Week.

Mr. Solidum said the adoption of technology-driven solutions to boost food production and improve supply chains has become increasingly important as Metro Manila continues to face rising food prices, making food affordability and accessibility a challenge.

He said food prices in Metro Manila have increased by around 40% to 50% over the past decade.

Among the crops suitable for Metro Manila are oyster mushrooms, which do not require large amounts of space to cultivate, according to Romelen T. Tresvalles, regional director of DoST-NCR.

To make mushroom farming more viable in urban areas, DoST, in partnership with the Rizal Technological University (RTU), developed the Solar-Powered Automated Modular Mushroom Growing House. The technology is designed for easy community adoption as it is inexpensive, easy to assemble, requires minimal maintenance, and features an automated system for mushroom cultivation.

A community in Pasig City is among the beneficiaries of the technology.

Ms. Tresvalles also said the agency is piloting an aquaculture system for catfish farmers in Valenzuela City and Muntinlupa City.

title: Dapitan: Where Rizal's stories live on
content_lead:
I was looking at an old farmer's clothing on display inside the NHCP Museo ni Jose Rizal Dapitan when I heard a voice from behind.

"Sir, that was the original clothing Jose Rizal wore when he went to his farm during his exile here in Dapitan." I turned around and saw Manong guard, who began telling me more about the clothes on display.

"During his four years here in Dapitan, he became a farmer, a doctor, an engineer, a naturalist and a businessman," he added.

Manong guard must have sensed my interest in learning more about our national hero because he began sharing little-known details about Rizal as we walked through the exhibits.

He told me how Rizal created a piping system that brought clean water from a spring to his kitchen, how he acquired the 16-hectare property where the shrine now stands using part of his lottery winnings, and how he had a son with his partner Josephine Bracken who died shortly after being born prematurely.

title: Vince Maristela, lumusong sa baha at umangkas sa trak ng bumbero dahil sa trapik
content_lead:
Pinili ng former Pinoy Big Brother Celebrity Collab Edition housemate at Kapuso actor na si Vince Maristela na maglakad na lamang sa gitna ng ulan kaysa maipit sa matinding trapik dahil sa bahang dulot ng malakas na pag-ulan sa Luzon.

Sa isang video na kaniyang ibinahagi sa kaniyang Facebook account, ipinasilip ng Kapuso actor sa kaniyang followers ang kaniyang pinamagatang "Baha Serye". Sa video, ipinakita ni Vince ang kaniyang karanasan sa paglalakad sa kahabaan ng Marcos Highway upang makaiwas sa traffic.

Ayon kay Vince, mas mabilis pa siyang makararating sa kaniyang pupuntahan gamit ang sariling mga paa kaysa maghintay sa loob ng kotse.

Ipinakita niya sa kaniyang video ang mabigat na trapik sa kalsada kung saan marami na ring mga taong ang pinili maglakad. Ipinakita niya rin ang mga nakalinyang mga sasakyan na nakatigil sa kalsada dahil inabot na rin ng baha ang daanan.

title: Marcos: 30 underground water catchment sites identified for flood control
content_lead:
Marcos says the water catchment projects would be prioritized, and excavation works would start as soon as possible.

MANILA, Philippines - Thirty sites for underground flood catchments have been identified, with excavation work expected to begin soon, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said following a situation briefing on Wednesday, August 19, on the impact of continuous rain.

Some of these sites in Metro Manila - Rajah Sulayman Park, Rizal Memorial Stadium, Camp Aguinaldo, and University of Sto. Tomas - were identified with the help of Dutch experts, according to Marcos.

"Kaya't mayroon na tayong tatlumpu na sites na puwede nating gamitin para dito sa mga cisterns at inaantay na lang natin 'yung detailed engineering," said Marcos. (We already have 30 sites where we can install cisterns, and we're only waiting for the detailed engineering plans.)

He said the water catchment projects would be "prioritized" and excavation works would start as soon as possible.

"We are already at present time conferring and speaking to whoever are in charge of these areas so they will allow excavation works," said Marcos in a mix of Filipino and English.

Other flood-control measures the Marcos Jr. administration plans to carry out include upgrading seawalls and establishing systems for the household and industrial use of collected rainwater.

Marcos held a situation briefing with the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority on Wednesday, along with some Cabinet officials, regarding the combined effects of the habagat and tropical cyclones Kuis, Maymay, and Neneng.

At least 27 people have died and 17 individuals were hurt as of Wednesday, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council. Agricultural production value loss amounted to P1.42 billion, affecting more than 40,000 farmers and fisherfolk.

title: Groups launch own SONA on food security, coastal livelihoods
content_lead:
VARIOUS groups from fisherfolk organizations, civil society and environmental advocates on Monday launched their own State of the Nation (SONA) to assess the state of the country's fisheries sector, among others.

The groups called on the Marcos administration to prioritize protecting critical marine ecosystems and biodiversity-rich seascapes from pollution and destructive development through the passage of the proposed Verde Island Passage (VIP) bill.

They also sought the passage of House Bill 5606, or the "Atin ang Kinse" Bill, to strengthen protection of the 15-kilometer municipal waters and uphold the rights of small-scale fishers.

They demanded the provision of comprehensive and sustained support for fisherfolk beyond piecemeal assistance and short-term relief, as well as the improvement of fisheries governance and investment in sustainable fisheries and resilient coastal livelihoods.

"The Marcos administration must push for the strengthening of local fisheries production to ensure food security and affordable fish for Filipinos and comprehensive support for small-scale fisherfolk through fuel, equipment, and post-harvest assistance," the groups said during the launch in Quezon City.

title: 'Protect our seas': Fisherfolk respond to Marcos' Sona
content_lead:
MANILA, Philippines -- A day after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. highlighted government aid for nearly 2 million farmers and fisherfolk in his fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona), municipal fishers had a message of their own: They do not want to remain dependent on subsidies. They want the government to protect the fishing grounds the law has long reserved for them.

Gathering in Quezon City on Tuesday, July 28, for what they called the "State of the Fisherfolk Address 2026," a kontra-Sona, or counter-Sona, small-scale fisherfolk leaders, marine conservation group Oceana, scientists, legislators, youth advocates and local government officials said Marcos' nearly three-hour speech failed to acknowledge what they described as the country's worsening fisheries crisis.

They argued that the administration continues to focus on financial assistance while leaving unresolved what they consider the sector's most urgent concern: the continued entry of commercial fishing vessels into the country's 15-kilometer municipal waters, which Philippine law reserves primarily for municipal and subsistence fisherfolk.

The forum carried a pointed theme: "Pangakong Kinse: Para sa mga mangingisda o para sa negosyante? State of the Fisherfolk Address 2026."

During Monday's Sona, Marcos cited government interventions during the recent oil price crisis, including the Presidential Assistance to Farmers, Fisherfolk and Families (PAFFF) program.

He said the government had extended support to nearly 2 million farmers and fisherfolk at the height of soaring fuel prices. He also highlighted Kadiwa markets, where farmers and fisherfolk could directly sell their produce, as among the measures meant to cushion the impact of the energy crisis.

title: DepEd, DILG sign IRR for Early Childhood Care and Development
content_lead:
To ensure quality early education for children, the Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday finally signed the implementing guidelines for Early Childhood Care and Development (ECCD).

This came after the DepEd signed the implementing rules and regulations (IRR) of Republic Act 12199, or the ECCD System Act, in partnership with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) at the Quezon City Reception House.

In a statement, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said the formal guidelines will help advance early childhood programs in coordination with local government units (LGUs) nationwide.

"Kung seryoso tayong baguhin ang kinabukasan ng Pilipinas, kailangan nating magsimula sa ating mga pinakabatang kababayan," he said.

This move adheres to the recommendations made during the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2).

Under the ECCD System Act, expanded access to healthcare, nutrition, and quality early learning will benefit children from birth to age 8.

With this in place, early literacy and numeracy alongside holistic development for children will be advanced from their early years.

"Dito nagsisimula ang tunay na nation-building," Angara said.

The DepEd said the way to boost foundational learning is to start before a child enters formal schooling.

Complementary to this, expanded access to more established Child Development Centers (CDCs) in low-income LGUs was also highlighted.

To date, P741 million out of the P1 billion allocated for CDC establishments has been released to 247 beneficiary barangays, under the Local Government Support Fund - Financial Assistance to Local Government Units.

As of July, 14 CDCs are fully completed, while 113 are under construction and 106 are undergoing procurement.

title: Philippine floods: Over P1 billion in agricultural damage as monsoon hits vegetable farms
content_lead:
Sixty-four-year-old Filipino grandmother Elia Jalota is currently staying at a crowded evacuation center in Bagong Silangan, Quezon City. Her house and water cabbage (kangkong) patch are flooded by the ongoing southwest monsoon battering the Philippines since the start of the month.

"We have somehow gotten used to this life already, living in evacuation centers whenever it floods," she told Khaleej Times.

Bagong Silangan is an urban poor community located on the edge of the Marikina River. Some of its residents, like Elia, raise water cabbages, sweet potatoes, taro and other lowland vegetables that thrive on the river's frequently flooded banks. The vegetable patches, however, have shrunk in recent years as billion-peso flood control projects have been built along the waterway.

The flood mitigation infrastructure projects for Bagong Silangan were prompted by the massive floods that hit most of Luzon Island in 2009. Typhoon Ondoy killed 36 residents of the community alone.

But even after billions of pesos were spent on these anti-flood projects, Elia's house and vegetable patch are inundated by the monsoons and typhoons.

Recovery assistance now

The Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP, Farmers' Movement of the Philippines) called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr and the Department of Agriculture (DA) to immediately provide production subsidies and recovery assistance to vegetable farmers hit by floods and continuous rains from the monsoon and typhoon weather disturbances.

As of Monday, August 17, agricultural damage has surpassed P1 billion (Dh60 million), including P589 million (Dh35.6 million) in rice and P313 million (Dh18.9 million) in vegetables, according to the DA.

KMP said vegetable farmers are facing a double blow: damaged crops and very low buying prices. Like grandmother Elia, whose crops have been inundated, they can no longer sell their produce due to bad weather and flooding
